newsitem.title: IRAN: Former Iran economy minister named to post again.
newsitem.headline: Former Iran economy minister named to post again.

text.p: Hossein Namazi, named by Iranian President Mohammad Khatami to be the Islamic republic's new economy and finance minister, is a university professor who first held the post over a decade ago.
The 53-year-old doctor of economics was named on Tuesday to take over the helm of the oil-dependent and inflation-ridden economy after spending several years in the job in the 1980s.
If approved by parliament, which will debate the merits of the 22 proposed ministers next week, Namazi will replace Morteza Mohammadkhan who has been in the position since 1993.
Namazi, who studied in Austria, held the post from 1982 to 1986 under then prime minister Mirhossein Moussavi, a radical exponent of a state-controlled economy.
Born in 1944 in the southern city of Shiraz, Namazi is credited with keeping the economy under firm control at a time of war and sanctions.

Despite the 1980-88 war with Iraq, Iranians have good memories of economic conditions then. Unemployment was low, subsidies were high and there was little sign of the corruption which is prevalent now, analysts said.

While in Europe in the 1960s and early 1970s, Namazi founded an Islamic society in Innsbruck, Austria. He was active with Islamist groups in Europe which opposed the pro-Western Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. He returned to Iran in 1975.
After the 1979 Islamic revolution he headed a body of Moslem university professors and held the post of chancellor for two years of an Iranian university.
He is fluent in German and English.

Political analysts have said many of those who voted Khatami into office were pinning their hopes on him to fight inflation -- officially put at about 20 percent -- cut 10 percent unemployment and steer the country towards prosperity.
But they say Namazi would have a tough task.
Iran, the world's third largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway, relies on oil for 40 percent of state income.
Even though the economy grew 4.5 percent in the last Iranian year to March, economists say it is not expanding fast enough to significantly outpace population growth.
Namazi will also have to deal with U.S. economic sanctions.
Last week Washington tightened its sanctions on Iran, saying it would punish firms spending $20 million or more a year in Iran's oil or gas sector -- lowering the trigger from $40 million.
